utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there was one short preliminary matter to be raised by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. This relates to MFI P7167. The Prosecution has received a revised English translation of P7167 MFI. It was discussed on the transcript at T32471 through 32473 on the 2nd of March, and 32480 through 32481 on the 3rd. The revised translation has been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0122-6836-ET. And if the Defence do not object, we would request that the Court Officer be instructed to replace the existing translation with the revised version and the document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. And, as always, if there's any problem, the Defence has an opportunity to revisit the matter once they've further looked into it. The Court Officer is hereby instructed to replace the translation as is now attached to P7167 by the newly uploaded one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. P7167. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I take this opportunity to note that the Prosecution is joined this morning by Mr. Matthew Gillett, who will be taking the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, welcome in the courtroom. It's the week of the newcomers, it seems, that's -- from both sides, so everything very balanced. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. I meanwhile deal with Exhibits P5969 and P5970. The Chamber notes that page 1 and 2 of the B/C/S version of Exhibit P5970 are identical to the B/C/S version of Exhibit P5969, while the English translations of both differ. Although the Chamber did not find substantial discrepancies, this is hereby put on the record. The Chamber leaves it to the parties whether they request for verification of the translations and, at the same time, leaves it to the Prosecution whether it withdraws one of those exhibits. If the Prosecution intends to do the latter, the Chamber remarks that Exhibit P5970 consists of more than two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to follow up on one point from our discussion yesterday and we were discussing the presence of Rade Bozovic and Serb DB units in your zone of operations. And it was Bozovic's unit -- it was part of the Red Berets in Doboj that you mentioned; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now in June 1992, the Teslic Brigade of the VRS co-operated with Red Beret units from Doboj in mopping up Muslim and Croat villages in Teslic municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Staying with Teslic, you were aware that thousands of Muslims and Croats had left Teslic by the end of July 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And they left because of the crimes that were being committed against them; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information, although crimes had been committed. But then since this Teslic Brigade was there that was guarding the town of Teslic, many families of Muslims and Croats left without any kind of torture because their villages and towns were there, where their people lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Teslic Municipal Assembly took a decision that any citizen of Teslic who had left the area before the 1st of July should be banned from returning; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that decision of Teslic. I'm not aware of it. It's possible, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32045. This is a set of decisions by the Teslic Municipal Assembly at the 16th Regular Session on the 6th of July, 1992. And if we could have point 12, page 3 in the English and 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what you're heading for, Mr. Traldi, but the witness said he was not aware of this decision. Before you put another decision to him and then tender it into evidence, wouldn't it be good to ask whether the witness has any knowledge at all. Because cross-examination can be used in support of the case of the opposing party, but, at the same time, should not be the vehicle by which we just introduce a whole new -- all kind of new documentary evidence in the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I take the point, Mr. President. At the same time, often a decision may be -- looking at a decision may support putting to the witness that he must have known about it and that's what I'm suggesting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You can do that. But let's -- let me be clear on -- there are limits to cross-examination, even if it is in support of the Prosecution's case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm directing your attention first to point 12, the decision that: "Any citizen of Teslic municipality, regardless of ethnic background, who for whatever reason left the area before the 1st of July this year, shall be banned from returning." Now we see that at the same meeting, immediately above point 11, there was a discussion of carrying out additional mobilisation of Serb citizens in July 1992 and addressing with criminal proceedings people who'd failed to respond to the call-up to military service. Based on your position and the fact that Teslic was within your area of responsibility, you must have been aware, first, of the decisions to conduct additional mobilisation and to initial -- initiate criminal proceedings against --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- against those who hadn't responded; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you were aware of other decisions taken at this same session. I'd put to you, you must also have been aware that a municipality in your area of operations was taking the decision to bar the thousands of people who had already left from coming back. You must have known that, mustn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no, because the decision of the Assembly of Teslic, this decision of theirs, was not given to me. I was not aware of this content of the decision, except for the part that has to do with mobilisation. I had not received this decision, as the commander there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic -- Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are opposed to having this document admitted because the witness doesn't know, and he did not take part in the work of this organ whose document is in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The witness has confirmed his knowledge of some portions of, and I've put to him that he must also have been aware of others. But it, certainly based on his evidence, isn't right to say that he has no knowledge about the document or about the conclusions therein or about the work of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The document is admitted. The witness has testified that he has knowledge of the content of at least part of the decision, which is sufficient for admission. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32045 receives number P7184.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7184 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P5145.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps Command, intelligence and security department, dated the 12th of July, 1992, regarding the situation in the area of Teslic, sent to the Main Staff of the VRS. And it's signed by Zdravko Djuric. Zdravko Djuric was an officer in the 1st Krajina Corps Command; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to the third paragraph, we see a reference to some of the people we discussed yesterday. We see the 1st Krajina Corps Command is describing, first, Ljubisa Petricevic as the former head of the Doboj military department and a captain first class. Does that refresh your recollection as to whether Captain Petricevic was a civilian or a soldier in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Petricevic was an officer in the Army of Republika Srpska. As head of the military department in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And also served as Chief of Staff of the Teslic Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was head of the military department in Doboj at that time, and it was later that he came to the unit of the operations group or, rather, he became commander of a battalion. He was not Chief of Staff of a brigade. He was the head of the military Department of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just to cut this short, he's clearly identified here as a captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we turn to page 2 in the English. And, I'm sorry, also in the B/C/S, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yeah, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Part of the answer of the witness referred to later. Later always requires that you know what the starting point in time is. Could you please include that in your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm going to try to be very focused here, sir. First, if you look at the fourth paragraph in the B/C/S, we read: "In addition to the members of the Red Berets and employees of the Doboj CSB, the following members of the Teslic Brigade were among those arrested." The first name is Captain First Class Ljubisa Petricevic, the brigade Chief of Staff. Next name, Ranko Sljuka, aka Narednik [phoen], the commander of the Military Police Company. Then Radoljub Sljivic, the then-chief of OBO, and five or six military policemen from the Military Police Company. Now, this is a report dated the 12th of July, 1992. First question as a matter of chronology, does this refresh your recollection that no later than the 12th of July, 1992, the men I had just mentioned were soldiers in the Teslic Brigade of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not discern what the witness has been saying. Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you have been asked to repeat what you just said. I think it may have been about Captain Petricevic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Petricevic at this time was head of the ministry or, rather, Secretariat for Defence in Doboj. The municipal Secretariat for National Defence in Teslic and the one in Doboj were under him. I had no authority over Petricevic because these are organs belonging to the civilian structures and it is only commands that can ask them for replenishment for material resources, et cetera. That was the only link. As for all the rest, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to be fair, sir, what I'm putting to you is that the corps command here is correct, that these men were soldiers in the Teslic Serbian Brigade at that time and that the information you're providing is mistaken. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. Well, these soldiers, yes; but Petricevic, no. The rest, yes. But as for Petricevic, he -- I mean, Captain Petricevic, he was head of the military department in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you said he became a captain later. At what time in your -- earlier, you said he had become a captain later. At what time in your evidence did he become a captain in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a captain, but later in the unit he was appointed battalion commander, but not in the Teslic Brigade. Rather, it was the Doboj Brigade. Sometime in the autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Finally, sir, I want to turn to your evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm done with this topic unless the Chamber has any questions in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Finally, sir, I want to turn to your evidence about the conversation you had with General Mladic. Now you said it was in the retirees' club in Doboj and that it took place in August 1995, and he told you that 2.000 people had been killed during the night. First, about how long, how many days or weeks, after the events General Mladic was describing did the conversation you had with him take place?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. It was the beginning of August 1992. Now I don't know how many days after this crime, that is to say, it was then, the beginning of August. Perhaps the 2nd, 3rd or 4th of August, 1992. Then General Mladic came to Doboj to the corps command to meet up with General Talic, the corps commander, and some other people who were with him. Probably because of that. But primarily he came to see what the situation at the front line was and to get brief information from the units of the corps, how far they've gone, what is needed, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now what were the units of the corps doing at that time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, you are recorded as having referred to August 1992 twice. Did you mean to say 1992 or did you have another year in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992, the beginning of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What were the units -- you said he had spoken to you, General Talic, and some other people who were there with him to get information about the units of the corps, how far they've gone, et cetera. What were the units of the corps doing at the time that General Mladic had this conversation with you? What particular actions was he asking you about?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the corps were involved in an offensive and the breakthrough of the corridor, Odzak had already been taken, Derventa was under our control, and the units were at the place called Bijelo Brdo and that is where the fiercest fighting took place between the units of the VRS and the HVO. General Talic then asked to be briefed about the situation on the front and what the needs were of the units for the continuation of these operations. I was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, could you nevertheless revisit the year, because yesterday's transcript says "1995," and also in the context of what we read, it certainly needs more attention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I made a mistake, yes, it's 1995. It's after the victims of Srebrenica, yes. Sorry, I have been saying 1992 all along, and, of course, I meant 1995. My mistake in terms of this year, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you just said during the same conversation you discussed the breakthrough of the corridor, said the units of the corps were involved in an offensive operation, that there was fighting between the units of the VRS and the HVO. Now, that's an accurate description of what the 1st Krajina Corps was doing in the summer of 1992, but it's not what they were doing in the summer of 1995, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but are we still talking about 1992 or 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The line of questioning is such to -- to address that matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll re-ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you were describing the conversation a moment ago. I asked what particular actions that the units of the corps were undertaking at that time General Mladic was asking you about. You said the units of the corps were involved in an offensive and the breakthrough of the corridor, said Derventa was under control, the units were at a place called Bijelo Brdo. And what I'm putting to you is: That's an accurate description of what the 1st Krajina Corps was doing in the summer of 1992. It is not an accurate description of what the 1st Krajina Corps was doing in the summer of 1995. And so the rest of the conversation that you're describing clearly relates to activities in the summer of 1992, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I got the years wrong. The question was about 1992 so I focused on 1995, but in -- so I concentrated on 1992. But in 1995, civilian authorities were being established. Most of the bank was under our control, and the area from Ozren was under attack from Croatian forces and our units were very busy. And in that sense, General Talic briefed General Mladic about the situation in that area of the front line, and in the municipalities, the civilian authorities of Republika Srpska were just being established.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now have you provided a completely different description of the rest of the conversation just now to the description you provided when I asked you just moments ago. I'd put to you that your recollection of this conversation is not reliable. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I remember that thing in 1995. I had just got the year wrong when the questions were about 1992. So I concentrated on 1992, forgetting that this was in 1995. The area of Posavina up to the Sava River was completely free. It was only my mistake about the year. In 1995, I remember very well what specifically happened in that briefing by General Talic of General Mladic. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, since you remember it very well, I'm going ask you about a couple of other details from it. Was Milan Martic present for this briefing?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you said General Talic was briefing General Mladic about the situation -- about the situation in the area of the front line. At what point in that briefing did General Mladic inform you and General Talic that 2.000 people had been killed during the night?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well when General Mladic came in. He was standing in the door. He hadn't even sat down yet. He said, Brothers, something horrible happened that shouldn't have happened, without my knowledge and my approval. And only then General Talic sat down and the corps commander briefed him about the situation on the ground. He didn't want any comments anymore. He just wanted General Talic to briefly report to him about the situation in the units of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So ... first, is it your evidence that General Mladic came in, said 2.000 people had been killed, and then you -- first, let me finish the question, sir. Is it your evidence that he came in, said 2.000 people had been killed, and then you, he, and General Talic essentially conducted business as usual?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't finish talking about when he came in and said, Brothers, something horrible happened and it shouldn't have happened, without my knowledge and my approval. About 2.000 people had lost their lives, were killed that night. Those were his words. And then we sat down, and then he started talking to the corps commander. It was a conversation between the corps commander and the commander of the Main Staff, and we did not interfere in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were retired. In your evidence, why were you at this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was retired from the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia because I had completed my years of service, but I stayed on in the Army of Republika Srpska, that's what General Talic asked me, in order to work with the civilian structures in the Doboj region. That's how I was at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So what they were discussing, military operations, wasn't in your area of responsibility. Your area of responsibility was about co-operating with civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What was Milan Martic there for? Why was he at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They knew each other well, Martic and General Talic and General Mladic. He must have been invited to come in and see the corps commander. I don't know why he was there and who invited him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you say you were told these people had been killed. You understood, in your evidence, that you were being informed they'd been murdered; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Who did you tell?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not tell anyone. I didn't need to. Later on, when I went around these secretariats for national defence and presidents of municipalities, they had learned something about the same thing that I did, and I told them about that meeting and that General Mladic said what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your answer. Did you not tell anyone that 2.000 people had been murdered, or did you tell secretariats for national defence and presidents of municipalities in the Doboj area that 2.000 people had been murdered, in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told them that's what General Mladic had said, that about 2.000 people had perished, were murdered. People from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in your previous testimony, the last few moments, about what he said, you didn't say he had explicitly referred to Srebrenica. What, in your evidence, led you to think that that was what this was about?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he told us when he sat down together with General Talic that that had been done around Srebrenica and in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, did you get an impression as to who the perpetrators of these murders had been?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. And I wasn't able to get any impression who the perpetrator of these murders might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You would have known, however, that people held at Srebrenica were in the custody of VRS and RS MUP forces before they were killed; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that from TV and from what General Mladic said at the command post of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you know, of course, that there have been a number of trials, here and in Bosnia, of members of the VRS and the RS MUP for the crimes in and around Srebrenica. You've never publicly stated what you know in any of those proceedings, or what you claim to know, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me ask the question very precisely. You've never publicly stated or stated in any of the many, many Srebrenica trials what you are claiming that you know about the mass murders, the genocide that was committed there, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nowhere, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay, sir, then this will be my last question. I'd put to you that you've never publicly stated it before your testimony on behalf of General Mladic for the same reason that your articulations and testimony about the remainder of that conversation has not been consistent this morning, which is that your testimony about this is not truthful. That conversation, as you've described it, did not occur. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present. I mean, at what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have perhaps a few questions. In your testimony today, you said that General Mladic told that without his knowledge and without his approval about 2.000 people had lost their lives, were killed that night. "That night" meaning the night before he came to you or before you met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a couple of days ago, the beginning of August. And these events in Srebrenica, that was sometime in the second half of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it was clear to you that he referred to murders rather than to combat casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he explain anything further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite honest, he didn't want to go into any further explanations and details. He briefly informed the corps commander, and all of us who were there heard it. And he asked the corps commander to briefly report to him about the situation on the ground and in the units of the corps. There were no extensive comments. He maybe didn't want to talk more about it. But that's what he said at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that the corps command had no knowledge, as far as you understood, but that General Mladic knew about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The corps commander knew as much as I knew, from some reports, talk, radio and TV broadcasts these days. We didn't know any more about it. The specific knowledge we gained was when General Mladic was at our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you're saying that you had only very superficial knowledge. You said "the corps command, or corps commander, knew as much as I knew from some reports, talk, radio and TV broadcasts these days." Does that mean before General Mladic told you about the 2.000 persons that had been killed that night, that there were already TV and radio reports about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Especially Sarajevo Radio and Television, the Tuzla broadcasts. That's what we followed and that's what we heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did these broadcasts tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In these programmes, it was said that it was a genocide of the Serbian army, several thousand people had been killed, that's what the programme said. Over several days they publicised these events in Srebrenica, and at some point it reached its peak. And then we heard from the horse's mouth, so to speak, from General Mladic, that it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because you earlier said the specific knowledge we gained was when General Mladic was at your headquarters. Now, what was the specific knowledge, then, in addition to what you knew already from the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What he told us was that 2.000 people had been killed the night before without his knowledge or approval. Only that. That was not even close to what the media were broadcasting a few days before he arrived Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did the media then broadcast which was different? Because you said earlier that the media said that it was genocide, several thousand people had been killed. What was new about it, what you learned from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's nothing new. It's just that these figures had been exaggerated. That's what we knew. It was impossible that that many victims had been killed without the knowledge or approval by General Mladic. We learned that the figures publicised were exaggerated. That's what we learned, General Talic and I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, General Mladic tells you that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this gentleman just can take the headphones off for a second, please. We have to intervene regarding the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please take off your headphones for a second witness. No, you can put -- leave your glasses on but ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you can check if he speaks English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you speak any English? Do you speak any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's an answer to a question I put to you in English. Could you please leave the courtroom for a second and be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't know whom to address. I take it that Mr. Sasa Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Sasa Lukic can probably say the same I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently there was a translation issue which we should not confront the witness with. But what is the issue, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the witness talked about numbers of killed in the -- Srebrenica, he -- that Sarajevo reported, he was talking about 8.000 people and more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll -- we'll verify that with the witness. And could the witness be escorted in the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you told us about what the Sarajevo media reported, and you said it was exaggerated numbers. Could you tell us again what were the numbers they were broadcasting, the numbers -- number of victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They mentioned 8.000, 10.000, and more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you said you couldn't believe that that many persons would have been murdered without the knowledge of -- and the approval of Mr. Mladic. Now, for 2.000, did you consider that possible and that that would have happened without the knowledge and without the approval of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that it could have happened even without the knowledge or approval of General Mladic because that's what he said himself. Somebody was working in an organised way and secretly from him, against him and against the Army of Republika Srpska and the Serbian people. That was my conclusion. That's the impression I got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You got that impression on the basis of what? Just on the basis of those few words that General Mladic said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So he didn't in any way refer to somebody working in an organised way and secretly. He didn't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, when you -- when you listened to General Mladic during this meeting in Doboj, did he use the term "Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He directly referred to Srebrenica as the place where these crimes have happened, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That crime happened in Srebrenica, and that's what he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And he used the word "Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, in -- if you try to recall correctly, was he referring to an event which took place the night before you met him or several days before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened in Srebrenica happened a few days before we met with him in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because - and this is page 19, lines 1 and 2 - you said a minute ago: "What he told us was that 2.000 people had been killed the night before without his knowledge or approval." Only that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was it the night before or several days before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That meeting was several days later, but specifically when he was in Srebrenica, those events, as far as he knew, had happened the night before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us several times today that there was no talk between General Talic and other officers and General Mladic about this message. He just said that, and then you continued discussing the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Mladic was obviously not inclined to go on talking about that. He moved to the specific subject for which he had come to the corps command, to find out about the situation in the units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your statement, paragraph 28, there I read the last sentence: "The further conversation revealed that he was talking about the events following the fall of Srebrenica." Now, in your statement, you say there was a further conversation about this issue. Which of the two is true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That further conversation was very brief, just a couple of minutes and then it was over. It was not an hour or even half an hour. I said "further," but it meant only a couple of minutes. He did not want to go into any more discussion, not even with the corps commander. That was his decision. They went on talking about the specific issues for which he had come to the corps command. That was very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But there was a further conversation about this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. While I was there, no. Those several minutes, that's what I meant. And then the corps commander proceeded to brief General Mladic about the situation in the corps. That took -- that briefing took one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand that, but I don't understand what you're telling us now, that there was no conversation. Only a few minutes. You said earlier today --this can be found on page 13, lines 21 and the following: "And only then General Talic sat down and the corps commander briefed him about the situation on the ground. He didn't want any comments anymore." That suggests that there was no discussion at all about the killing of 2.000 people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for these few minutes, I mean, it wasn't a long conversation. The general certainly didn't want that either. What he said to us briefly is what he said. And then Talic was supposed to report to him about the units of the corps. That is what was happening there on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And did General Mladic tell you during this conversation that the people who were killed in Srebrenica have been in custody of the VRS and the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question. Did he tell you that he had been -- and I'm addressing you. Did he tell you that had he been in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was there, yes. It's that day, when the civilian population was moving out. It was shown on TV too. Those children and women were being seen off and they were saying that they were going to Tuzla, and I know that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But his presence in Srebrenica, was that part of your discussion or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm telling you, during those few minutes, he said to us what I have already said, what had happened, what is terrible, the most terrible of all. And then after a few minutes that conversation was over and then he moved on to concrete matters. Obviously he was not inclined to talk about that, and there was no need to, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did he in any way refer himself to his presence in Srebrenica, apart from what you learned from the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on those days, on that day, when that was happening, he was in Srebrenica. That is how I understood him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was my question: Whether he told you that it happened on the day when he was in Srebrenica or the night before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It was my understanding that that is what he said and that in spite of that, somebody did that behind his back, and that was terrible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, is there any explanation as to, to kill 2.000 people in one night, that takes a huge effort. Did he say anything about whether it was a group or a person or what -- what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not. He didn't explain it to us. He was not in a good mood, and he was a bit angry too. And he certainly didn't want us to comment upon that because this was certainly weighing on his mind; but no, no, we didn't make any further comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And from the conversation, you took it that these were not combat casualties but these were persons that were intentionally murdered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People who had been taken prisoner had been killed. So it was prisoners that had been killed. That's that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he say anything or did you learn anything about if persons having been taken prisoners are killed, that requires an investigation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he say anything about any investigation that was undertaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't say anything. Not then. Whether something was done, I don't know, but he didn't say anything then, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you understood that the persons killed had been taken prisoners. May I take it that you mean to say that they were taken prisoner by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that I have ten to 15 minutes, but maybe I need little bit longer today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under the present circumstances, we'll follow your -- after the break, we'll follow your re-examination, but it's understandable that you would need a bit more time. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of what was announced, that is, photographs are to be taken, we need a bit of a longer break. That is, we'll resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. I have a very short issue I could raise, that is, a remaining issue from the testimony of Nedjo Vlaski; P6889. During the -- I'll leave it for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I have to address you, the camera is between us. I understand that you were informed that for purposes of a panoramic picture, that a photographer will be for two minutes with us. He'll enter the courtroom now and he'll make that picture. You're supposed to -- just to remain seated, as everyone is. Mr. Lesic enters the courtroom and will make his panoramic picture for the purposes of the web site of the Tribunal. The Chamber appreciates the co-operation by everyone in this courtroom. Mr. Lukic, if you're ready to re-examine the witness, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Colonel, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday my colleague Mr. Traldi asked you - that is transcript page 32531, lines 5 through 15 - whether General Talic knew about civilians passing through Doboj from Prijedor. Did you discuss that with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never talked about that. And I don't see why they would go through Doboj from Prijedor, when it was encircled. What year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you come a bit closer to microphone so that the interpreters can hear you better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Traldi also asked you whether you were a member of the War Presidency of the municipality of Doboj. Do you remember when you became a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After receiving the duty of OG commander, that is to say, 1992, the 15th of May, they said that the commander of the OG should automatically be a member of what they called the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How often did you take part in the work of that body?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, three or four times. I mean, when they call me, when they tell me, when they ask me to come. I took part about three or four times. But later on during operations, I was not allowed to do that. I was not able do that. That was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your task, actually, there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to attend as commander of the units in the area of responsibility, that is to say, in the territory of the municipality of Doboj. Just to be present, as commander, and if I have some remarks with regard to the work of organs, the secretariat, the municipality, I could present them there. I mean, no other plans were made. Military plans were elaborated by the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The civilian authorities of the town of Doboj, did they provide anything for the army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Secretariat of National Defence of the municipality was duty-bound to replenish units, to send extra manpower and food whenever requested by units. As for weapons and equipment, that was done through the military, through military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were also asked by my friend Mr. Traldi about the four Serbian Ss as symbols on the Serb flag.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: This sign, is it nationalist or is it a national symbol of a people?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the national symbol of the Serb people wherever they may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were also shown a set of documents stating that someone had been released from custody in order to go to the front. What was your position with regard to that matter or, rather, with regard to that question of people being sent to the front rather than remain in custody?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the position of all commands, and we had orders to that effect from superior commands, that soldiers who were taken into custody by the military police or the civilian police should be interviewed. If they had not committed a crime, they should be released and sent to their war-time units.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were also asked about a unit that was called Vukovi sa Vucjaka, Wolves of Vucjak. And you were shown a document, stating that from a certain period of time in 1992, they became part of the Army of Republika Srpska. Also, you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd just ask that the witness take his headphones off for the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But apparently the witness does understand some English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd forgotten, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Perhaps I could say very briefly that I was rising in relation to the characterisation of what the document showed, and invite my friend to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Would you consider that, Mr. Lukic. Otherwise we would have to ask the witness to leave the courtroom. But for the time being, of course, usually best is to quote literally from yesterday's transcript, if it was -- yes, it was yesterday. That avoids any further dispute about what was said. Witness ...

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we have document P03826.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first paragraph of this document, it says the battalion from the STO Prnjavor, from Vucjak, is hereby being resubordinated to the 327th mtbr and shall fully be incorporated into it. Do you know who they belonged that before that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, before that they were at Vucjak, independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I seek clarification about the word "independently." Mr. Simic, did anybody command this unit, the STO Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say anything to you because that was outside my area of responsibility. Prnjavor is pretty far away from Doboj. I had no connection to them, so I cannot answer your question whether they were or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like do call a video, P7173.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: We should play it a second time, maybe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it has not been translated to us now, but we have the transcript because it is the same portion that was played before. The witness was able to hear it in his language, and unless there's any insistence on it being played twice, we'll just remember or re-read the transcript in English. So, therefore, there's no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, we had an opportunity to hear General Talic here explaining the objectives related to the corridor. What was the humanitarian situation in the western part of the country?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my area of responsibility, there weren't any major problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in the western part of Republika Srpska around Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that I don't know. What I heard was that there were some areas that were critical, that is to say, imperilled from a humanitarian point of view. I learned that from the media. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection and to the best of your knowledge, is that also one of reasons why the corridor was supposed to be established?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. As far as I understood things, when preparing this with the corps command and in terms of the actual implementation, our conclusion was had there not been for a corridor, there wouldn't have been Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. S. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with this. And I have no further questions for you. I want to use this opportunity to thank you for responding to the invitation of the Defence team and for coming here to testify, both in my own name and the name of the whole Defence team of General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Yes, I first like to put on the record that the video we just saw, that the transcript of the text spoken is found on transcript page 32534 of yesterday's transcript. Judge Fluegge has a question before an opportunity will be given to the Prosecution to put further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to call up D921; page 5 in the English and the corresponding page in B/C/S. Mr. Simic, if you have now the hard copy of your statement in front of you, could you please have a look at paragraph 28. On the screen, it's the next page in B/C/S. I see here in paragraph 28 that there are some lines underlined. The words, according to your statement, spoken by Mr. Mladic. Why are they underlined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I did not underline anything. I made a statement to the lawyers of Ratko Mladic, and I didn't underline this. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also did not ask for it to be underlined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Traldi, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, in response to my colleague Mr. Lukic's question at transcript page 30 today, temporary transcript page 30, you said: "It was the position of all commands, and we had orders to that effect from superior commands, that soldiers who were taken into custody by the military police or the civilian police should be interviewed. If they had not committed a crime, they should be released and sent to their war-time units." Now, the Chamber has received the decision releasing the soldiers who we've discussed at some length. That decision says they confessed to the crimes. We saw that you'd signed the request to release one of them. So what I'm putting to you is: It was, in fact, the position of the command that soldiers who had committed crimes against Croats and Muslims be released and sent to the front. That's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the courts that decided if somebody committed a crime, they had to be held criminally responsible. The unit was not looking for those people. But the soldiers who have been proven not to have committed a crime, they had to return to their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, that was the last question put to you. This concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for treating me fairly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just one brief follow-up matter. We are looking into the document where there was an issue with the signature, my recollection is it's P7183 MFI, and looking into it with CLSS and hope we'll have something to report in the near future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And with that, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- what your report will be but we have to be patient. Is the Defence -- any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to ask to be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, Your Honour. And the next witness is Mladen Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Blagojevic, I presume. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Blagojevic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, please, tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mladen Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, have you given a written statement to the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to call up in e-court 65 ter 1D01663.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, you see before you the cover page of the statement. Can you identify the signature?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, do you recognise the signature and the date below?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is the date written in your hand?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we look at paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not hear any interpretation. Could you please restart, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, did you tell me during proofing that a minor correction needs to be made to make it more precise? In paragraph 6, in the second sentence, instead of the words "to the Suceska village," the phrase should be "toward Suceska village."

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 7, we should focus on the B/C/S. In English, it's also there. Did you tell me that also for the sake of precision about your movements, in the first sentence after the words "and General Mladic," we should insert: "With the said priest he went to the church in Srebrenica, and we from the military police platoon of the Bratunac Brigade went to the brigade command to refuel, and then we returned to the church in Srebrenica. After which, followed by General Mladic's vehicle, we went back to Bratunac. And then the general went to the church in Bratunac," and then the same text follows, "whereas we, in our own vehicle, went to the brigade command."

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after these corrections, now you have made a solemn declaration in this courtroom, if I were to put to you the same questions, would you provide the identical answers and would they be the best of your recollection about these events?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to tender the statement of Witness Mladen Blagojevic, which is 65 ter 1D01663.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1663 receives number D922.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D922 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I should like to read a summary of this witness's statement. Witness Mladen Blagojevic, in 1995, was a member of the military police platoon within the Bratunac Brigade. He remembers that on 13 July 1995, one squad of the military police was designated to escort General Mladic in the areas of Bratunac and Srebrenica. They moved about in a Pinz vehicle, and he remembers that within that squad there were eight or nine members of the military police. On that day, they followed the vehicle of General Mladic and his permanent escorts. They passed through Potocari into the sector of Suceska village where General Mladic addressed VRS troops and congratulated them on the operation they had successfully completed. After that, they headed for Srebrenica. And after refuelling at the brigade command, they returned to Srebrenica and then went to the church in Bratunac, and from there to the command of the Bratunac Brigade. The witness states that escorting the vehicle of General Mladic, they then headed toward Konjevic Polje. He remembers that passing through Sandici village they stopped for a while. General Mladic got out of the vehicle, seeing on the right side of the road about a hundred Muslims who had surrendered, he addressed them in a very conciliatory tone, telling them not to be afraid, that they would be exchanged for Serbs who had been captured. And he also asked them if there were any sick people among them, and if they needed a doctor, but nobody said anything. They continued on to Konjevic Polje, and there, they stopped briefly by the check-point manned by a few civilian policemen. He is not sure whether General Mladic got out of the vehicle at that time, but he remembers that through an open window or door of his vehicle, he yelled at those policemen because they seemed quite laid back, as if they were there to sun-bathe and not work. The witness emphatically maintains that the statement by Momir Nikolic about him talking to General Mladic at that check-point and that General Mladic motioned to him showing that the Muslims would be liquidated is untrue, that the whole story is completely fabricated. He is certain that on that day he did not see Momir Nikolic in Konjevic Polje, and he knows Momir Nikolic very well. He did not meet with General Mladic on that day at that junction, nor any other section of the road from Bratunac to Han Pijesak where they parted ways with General Mladic, who continued with his escorts to travel toward Crna Rijeka. That is a summary of this witness's statement, Your Honours, and with your leave, I have only a few questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we focus again on paragraph 6 of what is now D922.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to make everything perfectly precise, Mr. Blagojevic, can you remember in the sector of that village, Suceska, or the sector leading to Suceska, what was General Mladic saying to the VRS troops?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember. To the best of my recollection, General Mladic thanked the soldiers for the operation they had successfully completed. And in the end, he said to wash their feet and prepare to go to Zepa. That's what I remember General Mladic saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at paragraph 11 of your statement which reflects your recollection about the moment when you were passing through that intersection going towards Konjevic Polje. Can you remember around what time was it on 13 July?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, it was 3.30, between 3.30 and 4.00 p.m. Around 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in conclusion, where did you live after the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: After the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: After the war, I lived in Bratunac. And then in 1998, I moved to the United States because my wife's father and brother had been imprisoned in a Muslim camp called Silos and they had been registered by the Red Cross, and when the war was over, they could choose to live in a third country. They left in 1997, and they sent a letter of guarantee to my wife. She was the beneficiary of that letter. And in 1998 I went with my wife to live in the United States, and with my son, who was then 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you live in the US?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were entering the United States and receiving an immigration visa, did they ask you about your participation in the war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Before we left for the United States, we went to Belgrade and we had a meeting with IOM, that was the name of the organisation. We had to fill in an application form, but they tricked us, in fact, and they told us not to report any participation in the war for purposes of speeding up our immigration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So did you report your participation in the war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I listened to them and didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have problems later with the authorities of the US because of this?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have problems because under the US law, it amounted to an illegal entry, and there was even a trial there. I wanted to go back to my country, and that's what I stated at the trial, and I wanted to be deported.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So were you deported?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was deported in 2006. In November, I think, I'm not sure about the month. But I was deported into Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived at Sarajevo airport, I was arrested by SIPA and they told me that I'm a war crimes suspect. And in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was convicted to seven years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you serve that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Five years and 11 months is what I served. Thirteen months on probation. So I've done all of that. I was sentenced to seven years, but for as long as I live, I shall fight that judgement because I do not feel guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you not convicted of some of the charges that had been brought against you originally?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot remember how many counts there were, but I was only found guilty on one of them. And I repeat to you once again: I do not feel guilty in terms of what it was that the court in Bosnia-Herzegovina had sentenced me for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this completes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Before we continue, one very specific question. You said you were told not to report your involvement in the war in this application form. Was there any specific question about the involvement in the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As far as I can remember, the question was: Were you a member of an army, and if so, which one. And I said in that statement that I was in the JNA, but as for participation in the Army of Republika Srpska, I did not report that because these people from this organisation told me not to report that. And I'm not the only one, I mean, among all of us who left Bosnia-Herzegovina after the war and who went to America and did absolutely the same thing that I did. That is to say, it's not that I was afraid or something. During those eight years, I came to Bosnia-Herzegovina twice because my parents live in Bosnia. I came twice. So I did not go to America to hide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that in any way. But you were aware that you were not answering that question fully in accordance with the truth because you left out a certain portion. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That what's they told us to do, in order to speed up family reunification. But I did not realise that that was a crime according to American law, a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You knew that it was not the whole truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be cross-examined, Mr. Blagojevic, by Mr. Gillett. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Gillett is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, if you'll just give me one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, good day, Mr. Blagojevic. I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. If any of them are not clear, please let me know, and I'll do my best to clarify. Now, firstly, you've discussed your conviction for immigration fraud in the United States, and for that you received a 12-month suspended sentence of imprisonment; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure whether I was given that. When they asked me to go to court and to be involved in a trial with America, I asked for deportation. Now I don't know whether that was a judgement. I am not a lawyer. I don't know if you understand what it is that I'm saying ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get Exhibit P1517 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if we look at page 1 under the heading: "Verdict." And this is in both B/C/S and English. After we see your name and date of birth listed, if we skip three lines down, we see: "Previous conviction for immigration fraud in violation of Title 18, United States Code, Section 1546(a)." And then it says: "Sentenced to 12 months imprisonment." So do you accept that you were sentenced to 12 months imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I think that it would be fair to the witness to read what is written here in terms of the sentence to the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly you're referring to at this moment, Mr. Stojanovic. Is it a matter which cannot be raised in re-examination? Or let me see --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's not a problem. I think that that would be much shorter if he just read what is written here to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would follow that suggestion, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The relevant portion reads: "Sentenced to 12 months imprisonment, sentence suspended for deportation to BiH, arriving in BiH on 15 November 2006, held in custody pursuant to this court's decision." So do you accept that you were sentenced to 12 months' suspended sentence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I already said that to you. If that's a sentence, that's a sentence. But I'm telling you that I do not remember that I was found guilty. I was the one who asked for deportation from the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we now turn to page 2 of this document and in the first paragraph, the first full paragraph in English and B/C/S, we see the factual basis on which you were convicted. And it states: "On the night of 13/14 July 1995, at Vuk Karadzic primary school (now known as the Branko Radicevic School) in Bratunac, municipality of Bratunac, while there were several hundred civilian Bosniak men detained in the school, one of the Bosniak men appeared at the window of a room at the school, whereupon he pointed a Browning machine-gun mounted on a Pinzgauer at the window at which the Bosniak man appeared and opened fire from it, targeting both this man and the other Bosniak men inside the same room, while the bullets hit the window and the wall around the window." That's the factual basis on which you were convicted; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've already told you I was convicted of that, but I do not feel guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, a Browning machine-gun is a heavy weapon; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And would you accept that it uses 12.7-millimetre calibre ammunition which is a large-calibre ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And it can also be used as an anti-aircraft weapon; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, for this conviction in Bosnia for the crime against humanity of other inhumane acts you were sentenced to seven years imprisonment; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And that conviction was upheld on appeal; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'll come back to the events on 13 July 1995 in Bratunac in some time. Firstly, Mirko Jankovic, he was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade military police platoon that you were a member of in July 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And his deputy was Mile Petrovic; right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And Momir Nikolic was the chief of security and intelligence in the Bratunac Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So you knew all these people reasonably well in July 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: When you were carrying out your escort mission with General Mladic on 13 July 1995, did you see Jankovic, Petrovic, and Momir Nikolic in an UNPROFOR vehicle near Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, when you were being investigated for immigration fraud in the United States, you gave a number of interviews to US agents; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get 65 ter number 32111. And, Your Honours, I am aware the break may be approaching, and this will take some minutes to get through, so if it's a convenient time for you, I'm happy to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we are -- we came back to the courtroom at five minutes past 11.00, so therefore I think it would be better to take the break now and then deal with this matter after the break. Witness, we'd like to see you back there 20 minutes; we'll take a break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I resume what I earlier said about the issue remaining from the testimony of Nedjo Vlaski. P6889 was marked for identification due to an objection by the Defence with regard to the document's origin. This can be found at transcript pages 27822 through 823, and 27846. On the 20th of January of this year, the Prosecution advised the Chamber that the parties are in discussions about this document and asked the Chamber not to take any action before the parties have concluded their efforts. This is to be found at transcript page 30242. Are either parties in a position to advise the Chamber whether the discussions have resulted in an agreement in relation to P6889? I don't expect immediate answer but it is now brought to your attention again, and we'd like to hear from you still this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
